'''Gursaran Prasad'''{{Efn|Also spelled "Prashad" (see INSA profile)}} ("'''Pran'''") '''Talwar''' (born 2 October 1926<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Aggarwala |first1=Dharma Vira |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pkwbAQAAMAAJ&q=Gursaran+Talwar+2+october+1926 |title=All India Educational Directory |last2=Singh |first2=Gurbachan |date=1972 |publisher=All India Directories Publishers |page=1085 |language=en}}</ref>) is an Indian medical researcher who is known for developing [[vaccine]]s and [[immunocontraception]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Raghunath |first=Ranjini |date=2024 |title=The Industrious Immunologist |url=https://connect.iisc.ac.in/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Connect-December2024.pdf |journal=Connect |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=44–48}}</ref><ref name="sciam_1996">{{cite journal |pages=38–40 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0796-38 |title=Pushing the Envelope for Vaccines |year=1996 |last1=Mukerjee |first1=Madhusree |journal=Scientific American |volume=275 |pmid=8658109 |issue=1|bibcode=1996SciAm.275a..38M }}</ref> His discovery of a unique strain of bacterium, eponymously named ''[[Mycobacterium indicus pranii]]'' (MIP) led to the development of the first [[leprosy]] vaccine (commonly called MIP vaccine) in the world.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dogra |first1=Sunil |last2=Jain |first2=Sejal |last3=Sharma |first3=Ayush |last4=Chhabra |first4=Seema |last5=Narang |first5=Tarun |date=2023 |title=Mycobacterium Indicus Pranii (MIP) Vaccine: Pharmacology, Indication, Dosing Schedules, Administration, and Side Effects in Clinical Practice |journal=Indian Dermatology Online Journal |language=en-US |volume=14 |issue=6 |pages=753–761 |doi=10.4103/idoj.idoj_360_23 |doi-access=free |issn=2229-5178 |pmc=10718117 |pmid=38099011}}</ref> He is most popularly known for founding the [[National Institute of Immunology, India|National Institute of Immunology]], an autonomous research institute of the government of India, and the Talwar Foundation, a non-governmental organisation for continuing research in vaccines.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Balasubramanian |first=D. |date=2017-04-15 |title=Talwar's talwar against leprosy, TB and cancer |url=https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/science/talwars-talwar-against-leprosy-tb-and-cancer/article18058044.ece |access-date=2025-07-09 |work=The Hindu |language=en-IN |issn=0971-751X}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Talwar was born in [[Hisar (city)|Hissar]] (now a city in [[Haryana]] state, India). At an early age, his family moved to [[Lahore]] (now capital of Pakistan), where he grew up and completed his school education. His original aim was to study medicine and become a physician, but his father suggested that he continued in basic science. He enrolled in the Government College, Lahore for BSc course.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Raghunath |first=Ranjini |date=2024 |title=The Industrious Immunologist |url=https://connect.iisc.ac.in/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/Connect-December2024.pdf |journal=Connect |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=44–48}}</ref> The college was at the time affiliated under [[Punjab University, Lahore]] (becoming an independent university as [[Government College University, Lahore]] in 1997).<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=About – GC University, Lahore |url=https://gcu.edu.pk/about/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200822171733/https://gcu.edu.pk/about/ |archive-date=22 August 2020 |access-date=2019-09-16 |website=gcu.edu.pk}}</ref> During his college days, Talwar was captain of the college rowing team and won all competitions he participated in,<ref name=":1" /> the most notable being the Harper-Nelson-Manmohan Boating Race Competition of 1938.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://ia801404.us.archive.org/4/items/in.ernet.dli.2015.86252/2015.86252.Report-Of-The-University-Of-The-Punjab-1939_text.pdf |title=Report of The University of The Punjab 1939 |date=1939 |publisher=Punjab University, Lahore |page=44}}</ref> After completing BSc with honours in chemistry, he entered the main Punjab University to study master's in [[chemical engineering]].<ref name=":1" />

Talwar's first year in the university was at the time of [[Indian Independence Act 1947|Indian independence]] for the British empire in 1947. The colonial India was separated into India and Pakistan, and the ensuing political and social turmoils in an event known as [[partition of India]] prompted millions of Indians to flee from the new country and settled in mass refugee camps in Delhi.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rathore |first=Riya Singh |date=2022-12-29 |title=Embracing 'Refugee-istan': A Look at Delhi's Refugee History and Why It Must Continue |url=https://www.epw.in/engage/article/embracing-%E2%80%98refugee-istan%E2%80%99-look-delhis-refugee |access-date=2025-07-12 |website=Economic and Political Weekly |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Alluri |first1=Aparna |last2=Bhatia |first2=Gurman |title=The decade that changed Delhi |url=https://www.hindustantimes.com/static/partition/delhi/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240415210242/https://www.hindustantimes.com/static/partition/delhi/ |archive-date=2024-04-15 |access-date=2025-07-12 |website=The Hindustan Times}}</ref> It was from such a migrant camp that Talwar finished his final examinations and received MSc (Tech) degree from the Punjab University in 1948. In 1950, he received a scholarship for pursuing doctoral programmes in Europe, and chose France, as he later remarked, "because I had a leftist inclination … ''[[liberté, égalité, fraternité]]'' [the national motto of France]''.''"<ref name=":1" />

Talwar joined [[Pasteur Institute]] in Paris and for the doctoral degree he enrolled in the Sorbonne (the [[University of Paris]]). (Pasteur Institute does not award degrees and is affiliated with other universities for the degrees<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-01-23 |title=Doctoral Programs |url=https://www.pasteur.fr/en/education/programs-and-courses/doctoral-programs |access-date=2025-07-12 |website=Institut Pasteur |language=en-gb}}</ref>). He was initially assigned to [[Fermentation in winemaking|fermentation]] section to study on yeasts for making champagne. He did not like it, saying, "The first time that I tasted champagne, I wondered why it was so special. It had no taste. I was not interested." He was transferred to biochemistry section under the supervision of [[Jacques Monod]], who later received the [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine]] in 1965.<ref name=":1" />

After receiving Doctor of Science degree from the Sorbonne, Talwar went to Germany as an Alexander von Humboldt Postdoctoral Fellow (from the [[Alexander von Humboldt Foundation]]) and worked at various universities including at Tübingen, Stuttgart and Munich.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=INSA Indian Fellow |url=http://insaindia.org/detail.php?id=N74-0825 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150121093641/http://insaindia.org/detail.php?id=N74-0825 |archive-date=21 January 2015 |access-date=21 January 2015 |website=Indian National Science Academy}}</ref> In 1956, he came across an advertisement for the establishment of [[All India Institute of Medical Sciences]] (AIIMS) in New Delhi.<ref name=":1" /> He joined as an associate professor of biochemistry (1956), and later became professor and head of the department till 1983. He was appointed Head of the [[Indian Council of Medical Research]] (ICMR)-[[World Health Organization]] (WHO) Research and Training Centre in Immunology for India and South East Asia between 1972 and 1991). In 1983, the government of India instituted the National Institute of Immunology (NII) appointing him as the founding director and retired from it as professor of eminence in 1994.<ref name=":2" />

Immediately upon retirement from government service, Talwar was appointed professor of eminence and senior consultant at the [[International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology]] (ICGEB), a project of the [[United Nations Industrial Development Organization]] (UNIDO) started in 1983. He worked there till 1999. Among honorary positions, Talwar was visiting professor at [[College de France]] (1991), [[Wellcome Trust|Wellcome Professor]] at [[Johns Hopkins University|Johns Hopkins]] (1994–95), and distinguished professor at the [[Institute of Bioinformatics and Biotechnology]] and then at the [[Savitribai Phule Pune University|University of Pune]] (2005–10).<ref name=":2" />

In 1982, Talwar founded an independent research organisation, the Talwar Research Foundation in New Delhi. The [[Department of Scientific and Industrial Research]] (DSIR) of India officially approved it as Scientific and Industrial Research Organization (SIRO). Similar to Pasteur Institute, the foundation conducts research, especially in vaccine development,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Talwar |first1=Gursaran P. |last2=Gupta |first2=Jagdish C. |last3=Purswani |first3=Shilpi |last4=Vyas |first4=Hemant K. |last5=Nand |first5=Kripa N. |last6=Pal |first6=Priyanka |last7=Ella |first7=Krishna M. |date=2021-12-16 |title=A unique vaccine for birth control and treatment of advanced stage cancers secreting ectopically human chorionic gonadotropin |url=https://www.explorationpub.com/Journals/ei/Article/100326 |journal=Exploration of Immunology |language=en |doi=10.37349/ei.2021.00026 |issn=2768-6655|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Garg |first1=Himani |last2=Hada |first2=Rohit Singh |last3=Gupta |first3=Jagdish C |last4=Talwar |first4=G P |last5=Dubey |first5=Shweta |date=2018-12-20 |title=Combination immunotherapy with Survivin and luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone fusion protein in murine breast cancer model |journal=World Journal of Clinical Oncology |volume=9 |issue=8 |pages=188–199 |doi=10.5306/wjco.v9.i8.188 |pmid=30622927 |doi-access=free |issn=2218-4333 |pmc=6314864}}</ref> by which students can earn doctorates from affiliated universities.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-05-24 |title=Talwar Research Foundation |url=https://indiabioscience.org/orgs/trf |access-date=2025-07-12 |website=IndiaBioscience}}</ref> In 2000, he became its director.<ref name=":2" />

In a 1994 paper,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Talwar |first1=G. P. |last2=Singh |first2=Om |last3=Pal |first3=Rahul |last4=Chatterjee |first4=N. |last5=Sahai |first5=P. |last6=Dhall |first6=Kamala |last7=Kaur |first7=Jasvinder |last8=Das |first8=S. K. |last9=Suri |first9=Sushma |last10=Buckshee |first10=K. |last11=Saraya |first11=L. |last12=Saxena |first12=Badri N. |display-authors=8 |year=1994 |title=A Vaccine that Prevents Pregnancy in Women |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=91 |issue=18 |pages=8532–6 |bibcode=1994PNAS...91.8532T |doi=10.1073/pnas.91.18.8532 |jstor=2365427 |pmc=44640 |pmid=8078917 |doi-access=free}}</ref> his group demonstrated that women could be vaccinated to prevent pregnancy.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Aldhous |first1=Peter |year=1994 |title=A booster for contraceptive vaccines |journal=Science |volume=266 |issue=5190 |pages=1484–6 |bibcode=1994Sci...266.1484A |doi=10.1126/science.7985014 |pmid=7985014}}</ref>

==Awards and honours==
*National Award in Bio-Medicine by the Indian [[Ministry of Health and Family Welfare|Ministry of Health and Family Planning]] (1969)<ref name=":2" />
*Elected fellow of the [[National Academy of Medical Sciences]] of India (1969),<ref>{{Cite web |title=NAMS Fellows |url=https://nams-india.in/downloads/fellowsmembers/FellowsDatabase_upto2019latest%20(1).pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240701032013/https://nams-india.in/downloads/fellowsmembers/FellowsDatabase_upto2019latest%20(1).pdf |archive-date=2024-07-01 |access-date=2025-07-12 |website=www.nams-india.in}}</ref> the [[Indian National Science Academy]] (1971),<ref>{{Cite web |title=INSA :: Fellow Detail |url=https://insajournal.in/intranetinsa/fellow_detail.php?id=N74-0825 |access-date=2025-07-12 |website=insajournal.in}}</ref> the [[Indian Academy of Sciences]] (1974)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Indian Academy of Sciences Fellow's portal |url=https://fellows.ias.ac.in/profile/v/FL1974040 |access-date=2025-07-12 |website=fellows.ias.ac.in}}</ref>
*Sunder Lal Hora Medal by the Indian National Science Academy (1978)<ref name=":2" />
*[[Legion of Honour]] (Officier de la Légion d'honneur), from the French government (1991)<ref name="sciam_1996" />
*Indira Gandhi Priyadarshini Award (1994)<ref name=":2" /> 
*[[Padma Bhusan]], the third-highest [[Indian honours system|civilian award]] of India (1992)<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ilbs.in/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=332&Itemid=112 |title=Prof. G. P. Talwar, Former Director, NII |access-date=21 January 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150121093803/http://www.ilbs.in/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=332&Itemid=112 |archive-date=21 January 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
*Life Time Achievement Award by the Indian Immunology Society (1998)<ref name=":2" />
*Mastroianni-Segal Award by the [[World Academy of Art and Science]] (1999)<ref name=":2" />
*Elected president of the Indian Immunology Society (1973–77), the Endocrine Society of India (1978), the Indian College of Allergy and Applied Immunology (1979), the Association of Clinical Biochemists of India (1982), the Federation of Immunological Societies of Asia-Oceania (1992–95), the Indian Academy of Vaccinology and Immunobiology (1994–98), the International Society for Immunology of Reproduction (1995–98), and the 10th International Congress of Immunology (1998).<ref name=":2" />
